noticias.titulo: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
noticias.resumen: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
noticias.texto:
Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80

Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ãngel FÃ©lix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
FÃ©lix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.
Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', FÃ©lix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ãngel FÃ©lix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.
He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's MedellÃn Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the MedellÃn Cartel. FÃ©lix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under FÃ©lix Gallardo influenced Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.
In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena.
Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.
His death sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.
In 1989, FÃ©lix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was placed under house arrest since 2022 and died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.
In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' GuzmÃ¡n was introduced to FÃ©lix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.
From the subsequent break-up of FÃ©lix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by GuzmÃ¡n, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.
In 2019, GuzmÃ¡n was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.

noticias.titulo: Steering failure preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
noticias.resumen: Preliminary findings by National Transportation Safety Board investigators suggest the tanker suffered a "steering casualty" before colliding with the cruise ship on Friday.
noticias.texto:
Steering failure preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
- Published
The tanker that struck a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday had a steering failure, officials said, citing preliminary findings into the collision.
It remains unclear what caused the "steering casualty" on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday.
The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for.
The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them".
- New Orleans port files $1m lawsuit over 'miracle on the Mississippi' tanker collision 
  - Published10 hours ago
The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder.
Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders.
"We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference.
The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added.
A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days.
Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.
Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.
The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

noticias.titulo: Police ban protests near 10 schools and five universities in Paris
noticias.resumen: The order will be in place from 16 to 20 November, Paris police chief Patrice Faure says.
noticias.texto:
Police ban protests near 10 schools and five universities in Paris
- Published
Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.
The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".
A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.
Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.
Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.
Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.
On Saturday, 106,000 people from a range of groups took to the streets in France, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said.
It marked the fifth Saturday in a row where students, unions and yellow-vest activists went out to protest.
The number of protesters was much lower than previously, and so was the number of those arrested, the ministry said - 219 across the country, including 45 in Paris.

noticias.titulo: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
noticias.resumen: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
noticias.texto:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.
More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.
Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.
"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."
In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.
That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.
And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.
But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.
The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.
Restless tycoons
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".â¯ They had money, which back then meant power.
This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.
But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.
Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.
"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.
Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). â¯Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (Â£525bn).
But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.
Autocracy, oligarchy or democracy?
Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.
"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."
And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.
"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.
And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.
There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."
If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.
In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.
Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.
Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.
And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.
This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.
Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.
Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".
He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.
Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.
Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.
But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.
A bombshell interview
An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man.
Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him.
In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty.
But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world.
Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says.
The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin.
Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country.
No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen.
Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge.
Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia toâ¦ [an] absence of the future".
But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems.
Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man."
Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen."
Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

noticias.titulo: Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
noticias.resumen: Workers' rights, environmental concerns and local businesses remain at the centre of the debate.
noticias.texto:
Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
Workers’ rights, environmental concerns and local businesses remain at the centre of the debate.
Lusaka, Zambia – Zambia is attracting billions of dollars in mining investment as it seeks to become a significant supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition. But as foreign companies expand operations and new projects come on stream, questions are mounting over whether common Zambians are benefitting from the country’s growing mineral wealth.
President Hakainde Hichilema said more than $12bn had been invested in Zambia’s mining sector since 2022, as the government pushes to increase copper production and attract new investors.
Leading investors include Canadian companies First Quantum Minerals and Barrick Mining Corporation, India’s Vedanta Resources and China Nonferrous Metal Mining Group (CNMC).
Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH) has also emerged as a leading investor after committing $1.1bn to recapitalise Mopani Copper Mines, previously owned by Glencore. The investment gave IRH a 51 percent stake in the mine, with state-owned ZCCM Investments Holdings retaining 49 percent.
Alongside large-scale mining projects, the Copperbelt province has also seen the expansion of smaller Chinese-owned mineral-processing plants, some sourcing ore from artisanal and small-scale miners. Their growth has raised concerns about safety standards, regulatory oversight and environmental protection.
The government has sought to restore investor confidence through tax incentives and a more predictable fiscal framework, following years of frequent changes to mining tax policies under the former Patriotic Front government, which ruled Zambia between 2011 and 2021.
Unlocking mineral wealth and adding value
To accelerate mineral exploration, Zambia is undertaking a nationwide high-resolution aerial geophysical survey aimed at improving geological information and identifying previously unexplored mineral deposits. The survey is now about 98 percent complete, according to the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development.
The government has set an ambitious target of increasing annual copper production to 3 million tonnes by 2031, from less than 1 million tonnes in recent years.
“We can do with our copper, cobalt, nickel, lithium, manganese and rare earth metals, which we now know we have in this country for our people, what the UAE has done with oil and gas for its people and their economy,” Hichilema told delegates at the Zambia Mining and Investment Forum in Lusaka on October 19.
Beyond increasing production, Zambia is also seeking to expand value addition to copper, a key material in electric vehicles and renewable energy infrastructure.
Historically, the country has exported copper cathodes to China and other industrialised countries. But the government wants Zambia to play a more active role in the global transition to a low-carbon economy by developing domestic mineral processing and manufacturing capacity.
Africa’s two leading copper producers, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Zambia, are also exploring a partnership with South Africa to develop an electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry.
“DRC and ourselves are doing something on EV materials so we can build a joint venture with South Africa, which is ahead of us in the motor industry, so that the motor vehicles produced out of South African production lines have Congolese and Zambian inputs of the EV battery,” Hichilema said.
The proposed partnership reflects growing efforts by African mineral producers to move beyond exporting raw materials and capture a greater share of the value generated by the global energy transition.
However, turning these ambitions into reality will require more than increased mineral production. It will also depend on the development of local industries, skilled labour and infrastructure capable of supporting large-scale manufacturing.
Workers question their share amid mining boom
While foreign capital is driving an expansion of Zambia’s mining sector, trade unions say local workers are yet to see meaningful improvements in their working conditions.
“Inasmuch as the copper prices are going up and we have seen an increase in the amount of investments, we are experiencing same employment conditions – things are not any better for a mineworker,” Stephen Mwaanga, secretary of the National Union of Miners and Allied Workers, told Al Jazeera.
Despite higher copper prices, Mwaanga said, mining companies were also grappling with elevated production costs, including higher fuel prices, which he linked to the US-Israel war on Iran, affecting traffic via the Strait of Hormuz.
The wider Southern African region has also faced drought conditions associated with El Nino, putting additional pressure on electricity supplies. Zambia’s heavy reliance on hydropower makes the mining industry particularly vulnerable to reduced water levels, forcing the country to seek electricity imports and alternative sources of power.
Reliable electricity supplies are critical to sustaining the expansion of an industry that is central to Zambia’s economy.
“We need to strike a balance between improving the workers’ conditions of service and the challenges that these mining companies are facing,” Mwaanga said.
The challenge for the government is therefore not simply to attract more mining capital, but to ensure that increased production translates into better employment conditions and wider economic opportunities for Zambians.
Environmental costs of mining expansion
Beyond workers’ welfare, the rapid expansion of mining is raising concerns about its environmental consequences, particularly in communities already affected by pollution.
Eugene Mulenga, a human rights defender, fears the government’s drive to increase mineral production could place enormous pressure on the environment.
In February 2025, a structural failure at a tailings dam operated by Chinese-owned Sino-Metals Leach Zambia in Copperbelt released acidic, metal-laden mining waste into the Chambishi Stream. The pollution spread downstream into the Mwambashi and Kafue river systems, raising serious concerns about water quality, aquatic life and the livelihoods of communities dependent on the waterways.
A subsequent environmental assessment by the Zambia Environmental Management Agency documented the extent of the ecological damage and the effects of the discharge on affected waterways.
The incident exposed the environmental risks associated with mining expansion and renewed questions about the ability of regulatory authorities to monitor operations and enforce environmental standards.
Other pollution incidents have also been reported at mining operations, adding to concerns about the industry’s environmental footprint.
Zambia’s push to increase copper production to 3 million tonnes annually by 2031 has therefore intensified calls for stronger environmental safeguards and greater accountability from mining companies.
For common Zambians and local businesses, the benefits of the country’s growing mining investments also remain a subject of debate.
In an effort to ensure more mining-related spending circulates within the domestic economy, the government introduced local-content regulations, which require mining companies to allocate at least 20 percent of their annual procurement budgets for core mining goods and services to local suppliers in 2026. The threshold is scheduled to rise to 25 percent after one year, with further increases planned.
The policy is intended to strengthen indigenous businesses, create opportunities for Zambian suppliers and ensure a greater share of economic benefits from mining remains within the country.
But as Zambia positions itself to become a key supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition, the question remains whether the investment boom will deliver meaningful improvements in citizens’ lives, particularly those living and working in mining communities.
For Mulenga, the economic ambitions must not come at the expense of communities whose livelihoods depend on the environment.
“What we have discovered is that most farmers and poor people who depend directly on these water bodies near the mining sites are being affected by the increasing mining activity,” he told Al Jazeera.

noticias.titulo: Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling
noticias.resumen: Arab party members were reportedly arrested before Israeli elections based on unfounded evidence from the PM's office.
noticias.texto:
Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling
Members of an Arab-led party were reportedly arrested before Israeli elections based on unfounded evidence from the prime minister’s office.
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference.
Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government, launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government.
“The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election.
Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office.
Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12.
Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud.
The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded.
The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected.
“I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.
Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister.
On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power.
Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”.
However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

noticias.titulo: England stun Spain to end La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run
noticias.resumen: Spain suffer first defeat since March 2024 after losing 3-2 to England in Madrid despite grandstand finish.
noticias.texto:
England stun Spain to end La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run
Spain suffer first defeat since March 2024 after losing 3-2 to England in Madrid despite grandstand finish.
England held on with 10 men to record a stunning win over Spain in Madrid in one of the great UEFA Nations League games.
The visitors had seen their hosts parade their World Cup trophy on the pitch before the game, but raced into a 3-0 lead inside an hour, before being reduced to 10 men on 65 minutes and having to cling on in a dramatic finale to pip Spain to top spot in Group A3 on goal difference.
It was a record 10th straight away win for the Three Lions, and it inflicted the first defeat on La Roja since they went down 1-0 in a friendly against Colombia in London in March 2024. The 43-game run saw them crowned European and World Champions along the way.
England produced a stunning start and might have been ahead inside the opening minutes, but Unai Simon made a brilliant reaction save to claw away Jude Bellingham’s close-range effort.
The visitors were irresistible in the first half, pressing high and denying the hosts time and space to find their rhythm, and Spain were unable to register a shot on target in the opening 45 minutes.
England led 1-0 at the break after Harry Kane latched onto Elliot Anderson’s pass in behind and drew a foul from Pau Cubarsi in the box. Following a brief VAR review into Anderson’s challenge on Marc Cucurella in the build-up, Kane stepped up to convert the penalty.
He fired to the right of Unai Simon to register his 93rd Three Lions goal on his 127th appearance in the final seconds of the half.
The visitors doubled their lead eight minutes after the turnaround as Declan Rice’s curling corner was met by a powerful downward header from the unmarked Ezri Konsa, his Arsenal teammate.
The hosts were in disarray four minutes later, when some slick counterattacking saw Bellingham slot through into space on the right of the box for the on-rushing Ben White to drill a low shot past Simon at his near post.
The game changed 25 minutes from time when Jarell Quansah was dispossessed in his own half, and Anderson was shown a straight red card for denying a goalscoring opportunity by putting his arm on Lamine Yamal as he raced into the box.
After VAR confirmed the decision, Mikel Oyarzabal sent James Trafford – recalled in place of Jordan Pickford in goal – the wrong way to give the hosts hope.
They piled on the pressure and reduced the arrears further on the break on 75 minutes, when Yamal’s first-time cross from the right was swept in off the post by substitute Nico Williams.
La Roja laid siege to the England goal in the closing stages as they sought a goal to extend their unbeaten run and claim top spot in Group A3. But Trafford produced a stunning double save in stoppage time, diving to his right to parry a shot from Fermin Lopez, then somehow bouncing up to turn the follow-up from Aymeric Laporte around the upright.
England held on to secure first place in the group on goal difference after both sides finished on 15 points.
Both sides will find out their Nations League quarterfinal opponents next March when the draw takes place on Friday. England is set to face one of the three A-Group runners-up, other than Spain, while La Roja will face one of the other three group winners.

noticias.titulo: Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
noticias.resumen: The countries accuse Israel of preventing tents and other supplies from entering Gaza, despite the humanitarian crisis.
noticias.texto:
Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
The countries accuse Israel of preventing tents and other vital supplies from entering Gaza, despite the humanitarian crisis.
Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom have urged Israel to allow immediate and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza, highlighting that recent floods have “brought further suffering” for Palestinians living there.
The countries’ foreign ministers co-signed Sunday’s joint statement, the latest international warning about the dire humanitarian situation in the besieged territory.
“People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance,” the statement said. “Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza.”
For years, Israel has restricted entry and exports into Gaza, home to more than 2 million people.
But since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, Israel has placed the Palestinian territory under a full-scale blockade, limiting access to even essential supplies like food and water.
Under the Geneva Convention, denying civilians access to humanitarian aid can constitute a war crime.
“We today urge the Government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” Sunday’s statement said.
Heavy rain this month swept away tens of thousands of tents in the territory, leaving many without shelter.
“This situation is entirely reversible”, Sunday’s statement said, “and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in”.
More than 1.9 million people have been displaced in Gaza, according to the United Nations, many of them suffering displacement multiple times.
As of November 1, the Global Shelter Cluster, a humanitarian organisation that coordinates with the Red Cross and the UN, estimated that Gaza residents need at least 1.7 million mattresses and 121,000 tents to face this season’s cold, rainy weather.
During Israel’s genocidal war, entire neighbourhoods and cities were levelled. Some of the structures that remain are unstable.
In September, at least 20 people were killed when a building they were sheltering in collapsed.
Shelter is only one factor in the ongoing humanitarian crisis, though.
Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war. The price of basic goods has soared as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege.
Sunday’s statement follows a similar appeal from the UN’s Humanitarian Country Team of the Occupied Palestinian Territory on Friday.
“The devastating impact of the latest rainstorm in Gaza was preventable,” the team wrote.
“Children and adults were killed, critical services suspended, and thousands of family shelters flooded, swept away, or torn apart – not by the storm alone, but by policy decisions.”
The European Union also released a statement on Saturday, expressing “grave concern” over the humanitarian crisis.
It urged Israel to “allow immediate, unimpeded access” to humanitarian aid and “reopen all Gaza border crossings”.
Sunday’s joint appeal also called on all parties to “implement the Comprehensive Plan for Gaza”, a plan unveiled in 2025 that called for an immediate ceasefire between Israel and Hamas.
But attacks have continued, including on Thursday, when an Israeli air strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed six Palestinians.
Israel is the subject of an ongoing genocide case before the International Court of Justice, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, have been issued arrest warrants by the International Criminal Court.
They have been accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

noticias.titulo: US Treasury chief calls for outsider to lead embattled tech firm Nvidia
noticias.resumen: Scott Bessent gives Nvidia's board 10 days to show the company's compliance with US export controls.
noticias.texto:
US Treasury chief calls for outsider to lead embattled tech firm Nvidia
Scott Bessent gives Nvidia’s board 10 days to show the company’s compliance with US export controls.
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an outsider to take the helm at Nvidia, the California-based technology giant that has faced scandal over its former chief executive, Jensen Huang.
Speaking on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures programme, Bessent said the company should look beyond its own ranks for Huang’s successor.
“This makes me think that, as the board conducts a search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company,” Bessent told Fox News. “Just [with] what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Bessent’s comments come three days after Huang stepped down on Thursday, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia plays a leading role in producing chips and other computing components for artificial intelligence (AI).
As a result, the company has been at the centre of a technology race between the US and China, with the two superpowers competing for dominance in the growing AI sector.
Huang was long a key figure at Nvidia, as one of the company’s cofounders. Since 2025, he has also cultivated a close relationship with the second administration of US President Donald Trump.
In August 2025, for instance, Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on the sale of H20 microchips to China, in exchange for the US government taking 15 percent of the sales.
But in late October, The New York Times revealed Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s clients.
The report cited unnamed US intelligence agents who believed Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to help the country’s firms navigate US chip restrictions.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Beijing has denied the allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims. She reportedly left Megaspeed in 2025.
Tightening chip controls
For his part, Jensen Huang had long maintained that wider access to US technology would help Washington preserve its edge in the global AI race.
Bessent, however, questioned whether Nvidia had turned a blind eye to potentially illicit chip sales to bolster its financial results.
In Sunday’s television appearance, Bessent suggested a 10-day deadline for the company to show its compliance with US export controls.
“I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel,” Bessent said.
“I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?”
The controversy has encouraged a bipartisan push in Congress to tighten controls on US chip exports to China.
Lawmakers, including Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, have sought to use the annual end-of-year defence bill to close loopholes that Chinese companies can exploit to obtain advanced US-designed semiconductors.
But Bessent questioned the need for new laws, telling Fox News host Larry Kudlow that Washington’s existing export controls were sufficient but needed better enforcement.
“I don’t think we need the legislation,” he said. “We have all the rules we need; we just need them enforced.”
A new leader for Nvidia?
Since Huang’s departure, rumours have swirled about who might replace him at Nvidia’s helm.
The company’s board has floated Rene Haas, the chief executive of the semiconductor firm Arm Holdings, as a possible successor to Huang, according to the Financial Times.
Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, having spent several years at the company before joining the British chip designer.
Trump, meanwhile, has named former Apple chief executive Tim Cook as a potential candidate.
In a post on Truth Social on Thursday, Trump praised Huang’s work at Nvidia and said Cook was an ideal candidate to replace him.
“A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote.
But the Financial Times has suggested Huang may seek to return to his top-level post. In a report on Sunday, the publication said unnamed allies of his are rallying Silicon Valley executives to support his return to the company.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” one source told the Financial Times.
Currently, chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading Nvidia on an interim basis.

noticias.titulo: Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
noticias.resumen: The pope has called for the preservation of Indigenous traditions in Peru as he wraps up a 12-day tour of Latin America.
noticias.texto:
In Pictures
Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
The pope calls for the preservation of Indigenous traditions in Peru as he wraps a 12-day tour in Latin America.
Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon.
Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which has seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina already.
The pontiff spent the morning in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire, delivering a speech at the Indigenous fortress of Saqsaywaman.
In his remarks, Leo praised the region’s traditional festivities and processions, which often blend Indigenous and Catholic spirituality.
“The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way,” he said.
Huge crowds also packed Cusco’s central Plaza de Armas to greet Leo. Though born in the United States, Leo acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, after living in the country for years and later becoming the bishop of Chiclayo, a major city in the north.
Leo is the first Peruvian citizen to become pope.
The visit to Cusco, a high-altitude city some 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested the 71-year-old pope’s stamina as he continues to recover from lung cancer surgery.
Leo, however, has shown no sign of fatigue since his 12-day, three-nation South American trip began on November 6.
In the afternoon, Leo flew to Pucallpa, a city near Peru’s eastern border, on the banks of the Ucayali River.
Pucallpa is considered a gateway to the Peruvian Amazon, and during his stay, Leo reinforced his late predecessor Pope Francis’s teachings on protecting the environment.
He also denounced the violence faced by Indigenous land defenders, who use their advocacy to confront deforestation, pollution and the threat of Indigenous expulsion.
“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said. “The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice.”
Indigenous communities have long been threatened by illegal mining, deforestation and other forms of exploitation. Mining has also led to a water crisis in Peru, with pollution leading to an increased risk of heavy metal poisoning.
Leo is expected to return to Rome on Monday.

noticias.resumen: Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data breached in cyber-attack but recommends customers update passwords Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised. Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating the incident with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.
Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating the incident with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts.
“Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange.
“We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems.
“Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.”
Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”.
“We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said.
“We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.”
Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they receive unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links.
More details soon …

noticias.titulo: Australia, UK, Canada and Italy urge Israel to allow critical aid to Gaza ahead of winter
noticias.resumen: Four countries call situation ‘entirely reversible’ in joint statement as flooding exacerbates humanitarian crisis Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and Italy have urged Israel to allow critical humanitarian aid to enter Gaza, describing the situation on the ground as “dire”. The four countries released a joint statement on Monday morning, urging Israel to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies being held at the border into Gaza ahead of winter. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and Italy have urged Israel to allow critical humanitarian aid to enter Gaza, describing the situation on the ground as “dire”.
The four countries released a joint statement on Monday morning, urging Israel to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies being held at the border into Gaza ahead of winter.
“We, the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom, are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire,” the statement said.
“The recent floods have brought further suffering – and this was only the first storm of the winter. People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance.”
The ministers said Israel had time to act “before the winter fully sets in”.
“This situation is entirely reversible … we today urge the government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” the foreign ministers said.
“The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.”
Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms in the past week. Thousands more have been left without shelter while sanitation infrastructure has also been destroyed by storms.
At least four Palestinian children and a woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents.
Australia’s Greens leader and foreign affairs spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said “harsh words” from the government would do little and that Labor should instead take concrete action.
“The Israeli government has not responded to harsh words from Australia before, they won’t now. Material action, sanctions on the war cabinet, ending the two-way arms trade, implementing sanctions on illegal settlements as other nations have done. These are real actions the Albanese government can take but has failed to,” Shoebridge said.
Shoebridge said Australia previously refused to join commitments by multiple allies including the UK that called for import bans on trade from illegal Israeli settlements.
“When it was a statement committing to material action, Australia disappeared,” he said on Monday.
Nasser Mashni, the president of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, said the criticism from Australia and other countries should be followed by action against Israel, including further sanctions, an import ban on trade from illegal settlements and a two-way arms embargo.
“As we enter the fourth year of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, Israel deliberately continues to make Palestinians suffer,” Mashni said.
“Palestinian families are struggling to keep their children warm in flood-soaked tents while Israel continues to obstruct humanitarian aid. Penny Wong’s expressions of concern are meaningless without concrete action.
“International law demands action, not more empty words.”
The group of foreign ministers urged all parties to implement the comprehensive plan for Gaza, respect the ceasefire and “their obligations under international humanitarian law” and allow “aid to reach the people who need it”.
On Monday, the Australian cabinet minister Madeleine King told ABC radio the four nations had worked on the statement.
“This particular group has been working on this kind of statement for a little while to make sure that people that are affected by the war in the Middle East can receive the assistance they need,” she said.
“But, really importantly … is the fact that this humanitarian aid will be able to be delivered.”
Comment was being sought from the Israeli ambassador to Australia.

noticias.titulo: Prince Harry tells Ukrainians they are ‘going to win war’ on surprise trip to Lviv
noticias.resumen: Duke of Sussex meets wounded veterans in city and says country could one day host Invictus Games Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country. The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country.
The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday.
It is the British army veteran’s fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.
He spoke at a conference organised by the Superhumans Center, a clinic in Lviv that specialises in care and rehabilitation of those who have fought in the conflict. The prince has previously supported the group, which provides prosthetic limbs to those who have lost them in battle.
He said: “Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success.”
Harry watched wheelchair rugby players who hope to be in Ukraine’s team at next year’s Invictus Games, which will take place in Birmingham. Ukraine is aiming to send about 60 competitors to the event – its largest ever team.
The prince said the games for wounded military veterans, which he set up in 2014, could one day be held in Ukraine. “When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” he promised.
At the rugby match, Harry hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, who took part in the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. The 41-year-old, who uses prosthetic legs, said he was “still an active serviceman”, and the prince expressed surprise he found time to train.
Odainyk said afterwards he had told Harry his involvement in his sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games”.
The prince visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, in September 2025 and in April this year. During the April visit, he called Ukraine “a country bravely and successfully defending Europe’s eastern flank” and said “it matters that we don’t lose sight of the significance of that”.
The 42-year-old spent a decade in the British army and served in Afghanistan, including as a helicopter pilot. He has described those years as the happiest of his life.

noticias.titulo: Digital finance products used to abuse almost 20% of young women and girls, UK report finds

Abusers are exploiting banking apps, online payments and digital credit to control young women, causing financial harm and preventing them from leaving relationships, according to research from the charity Surviving Economic Abuse. In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 080
noticias.texto:
Almost one in five young women and girls in the UK have experienced digital financial products being used as a tool of abuse by a current or former partner, a report has found.
Abusers are exploiting banking apps, online payments and digital credit to control young women, causing financial harm and preventing them from leaving relationships, according to research from the charity Surviving Economic Abuse.
Research for a new report from the charity, Access Denied, Futures Derailed, involved carrying out a nationally representative survey of young women and teenage girls, with Ipsos UK.
It found that almost one in five teenage girls and young women aged 16-24 in the UK – equivalent to nearly 700,000 people – had been affected by this form of abuse. One in three young women experience economic abuse. Rates are highest among disabled young women and those with caring responsibilities for children, with perpetrators exploiting additional vulnerabilities to exert control.
The research found that one in eight girls and young women had experienced a current or ex-partner preventing them from having login information, such as passwords for online banking, while the same number had experienced an abuser controlling their digital wallets.
It also found 7% of respondents had experienced an abuser taking out credit in their name without their consent or because they were scared to refuse, including from “buy now, pay later” lenders.
More than 40% of those who had experienced abuse said it had caused them financial difficulty, while half said it had had a negative impact on their mental health, such as anxiety, depression, panic attacks, self-harm or suicidal thoughts.
More than a third said the economic abuse prevented them from leaving a relationship with the abuser, and one in six had had to borrow money, including from digital lenders such as “buy now, pay later” and online payday lenders, to cover essential items or bills.
Becky* met her now ex-partner when she was 18 and was trapped in a relationship with him for more than a decade, during which time he isolated her from her family and friends, coerced her into more than £40,000 of debt, and prevented her from working.
Even though she fled nearly seven years ago, she continues to live with the impact of his abuse to this day. “I had good credit at the time and he didn’t,” she said. “Even though I said no, he broke me down over many months and forced me to take out a loan in my name to pay for a holiday that he wanted to go on.”
She said that he also obtained “buy now, pay later” loans in her name, which she only found out about when letters came through the post. “There was no verification, it seemed like all he needed from my address and date of birth,” she said, adding that when she left the relationship, the interest on the debt “was huge”.
“I had to access an [individual voluntary arrangement] but this destroyed my credit score,” she said. “When I fled, it was a huge struggle. I couldn’t get a phone or wifi.”
As it was her first proper relationship, she said she “didn’t know what was healthy or not healthy”, adding: “He also isolated me from my family and friends, so I had no one to reach out to. I wish that the government would make sure there is education about economic abuse in schools and in colleges.
“We also need to see banks building in extra layers of protection, particularly with the rising use of AI, they need to be responding to evolving perpetrator tactics.”
Experts and survivors are calling on ministers to use its promised financial education curriculum to educate young people about economic abuse. They are also asking financial services to remove opportunities for domestic abusers to exploit digital financial products and create additional protections to support survivors, including when adopting AI into their systems and processes.
Sam Smethers, the chief executive of Surviving Economic Abuse, said digital financial products could be “weapons of abuse”.
“To halve violence against women and girls, we must tackle abuse where it happens, including through the digital financial products young women use every day,” she added.
“We also want to see financial services firms working with survivors and experts to design out abuse of digital financial products and build in protections. Without action, we risk leaving hundreds of thousands of young women to pay the price.”
The minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Satvir Kaur, said: “This report shines an important light on a type of abuse that too often goes unrecognised and can take many forms, from controlling someone’s money, to their choices, to their future.”
“This government has set the unprecedented ambition to halve violence against women and girls in a decade,” Kaur added. “Through our ‘Enough’ campaign, we are working with partners across society, including the banking sector, to help people recognise the signs of economic abuse, challenge abusive behaviour and support victims to access the help they need and deserve.”
*Name has been changed
- In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org

noticias.titulo: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart
noticias.resumen: Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece , with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February. “We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women
noticias.texto:
Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.
“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”
The idea came from Benoit Swan Pouffer, artistic director of Rambert, which celebrated its centenary this year with a commitment to bringing in new audiences, in part by reinventing familiar titles, as in its dance version of Peaky Blinders. “Dance needs to be democratised and this is the way to do it,” said Pouffer, who is choreographing It’s a Sin.
Davies has a cameo in the trailer, although his own dance career peaked with a performance for Princess Diana with West Glamorgan youth theatre (she told him he should continue to “Dance, dance, dance!”). The dancefloor, however, has always been an inspiration. “They’re such potent places, so loaded with potential.” Davies spent many nights in the clubs of Manchester’s Canal Street, watching lives play out to music. “Those dancefloors were places of such extraordinary freedom,” he said. “Especially in the 80s, with that layer of secrecy. That’s where you’d be out – you might not be out at home – becoming the person you aspired to be.”
The dance world was notably affected by the Aids epidemic. “I had friends and colleagues who left us too early,” said Pouffer. He was dancing in the US in the mid-90s, and saw as much stigma about HIV and Aids in the dance world as anywhere else. “There was shame, it was hidden. Even Alvin Ailey, that’s not what we said [that he died of an Aids-related illness] when he passed. Even now there is still a stigma,” said Pouffer. “The trauma, you put it in a little capsule and you don’t talk about it. Now we have this young PrEP generation who don’t know how traumatic it was. The closest they can think of is Covid,” he suggested. “Remember in the beginning when we didn’t know anything about the virus?”
Pouffer also wants to convey the excitement and creative spark of the era. “The fashion, the music, the dance of the 80s, it was one of the peaks of history,” he said. There will be video and narration to help tell the story, with scripts by Kaite O’Reilly. Davies is an executive producer, as are Pet Shop Boys, whose title song will feature alongside an original soundtrack by Roman GianArthur.
When Davies originally pitched the TV series he was turned down by all the major UK networks, even Channel 4, which eventually commissioned it. “It was simply an assumption that it would be miserable, even when they had the first script to read,” he said.
The series went on to be a huge hit. “Not a week goes past without someone stopping me in the street,” said Davies. Yet it was hard to celebrate, “because no matter how proud we were, it’s a story that’s founded on a lot of deaths”.
There is “a great heaviness at the heart of it, a great sadness and loss,” he continued. “But we told it with joy and vigour and life. The most important thing is to remember the life that those people had, not the death … I think the show worked because it turned around and said: ‘Hey, we loved those boys. Remember the love.’”
- It’s a Sin is on tour from 16 February to 13 November 2027

noticias.titulo: US officials recover audio from ‘Mississippi miracle’ cruise ship and tanker crash
noticias.resumen: Tank vessel suffered sudden steering failure two minutes before slamming into docked riverboat near New Orleans Federal safety investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) recovered audio and released a preliminary timeline on Sunday of a collision between a cruise ship and a tanker vessel in the Mississippi River on Friday. The data was retrieved after more than 30 people were injured when a tanker collided with a docked cruise ship – American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage riverboat – near the port of New Orleans on Friday at about 12.30pm.
