noticias.texto:
Federal safety investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) recovered audio and released a preliminary timeline on Sunday of a collision between a cruise ship and a tanker vessel in the Mississippi River on Friday.
The data was retrieved after more than 30 people were injured when a tanker collided with a docked cruise ship – American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage riverboat – near the port of New Orleans on Friday at about 12.30pm. All passengers aboard the cruise ship have been accounted for, officials said.
The tank vessel suffered a sudden steering failure two minutes before slamming into the docked riverboat, causing it to tip on to its side, officials said.
“It experienced the steering casualty, resulting in the rudder remaining to starboard,” said Bart Barnum, senior marine accident investigator for the NTSB’s office of marine safety, during a media briefing on Sunday. “Following the steering casualty, the Atlantic Asphalt veered to starboard toward the east bank of the river.”
Before the collision, audio collected by officials captured “the ship’s whistle, warnings and requests for assistance broadcasted over the vessel’s marine radio, commands to deploy the vessel’s anchors, and emergency ship handling orders”, according to Barnum.
The NTSB is leading the safety investigation alongside the US Coast Guard, as well as American Cruise Lines and representatives from the Republic of the Marshall Islands, the tanker’s flag state.
A preliminary report is expected to be published within 30 days.
Images and videos of the collision have been circulating online. The father of a cruise ship worker who survived the collision spoke about the moment his daughter called him in the middle of the incident.
“She’s FaceTiming me hysterically in a lifejacket in the middle of the Mississippi River crying, ‘Dad, dad, I had to jump off the boat,’” said Wayne Hager in an interview with Good Morning America over the weekend. “I’m hearing people screaming and yelling in the background and kind of like some, I don’t know, like metal grinding noises or whatever.”
Video of Leelah Hager posted on social media later shows her in the water wearing a life vest immediately after the collision between the Atlantic Asphalt tanker and the cruise ship, which had about 190 passengers and crew aboard. Other images of the incident show how the tanker caused the American Heritage to capsize.
New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit seeking more than $1m in damages from the owner and operator of the asphalt tanker. Four crew members of the American Heritage filed a separate lawsuit against Nave Shipping and Thome Ship Management, which oversee the tanker, claiming they “suffered significant and life changing injuries to their mind and body”, according to the suit.
According to the document, the collision caused the cruise ship to partially sink, throwing the crew members and passengers of the American Heritage “overboard into the Mississippi River, not knowing if they were going to live or die”, the lawsuit reads.
The crew members of American Heritage are alleging negligence, gross negligence, carelessness or fault of the managers of the tanker.

noticias.titulo: Somali-American Uber driver brutally assaulted in alleged hate crime in Minnesota
noticias.resumen: Mohamed Yusuf is fighting for his life after alleged attack by passenger who said he did not like driver’s first name A Somali-American Uber driver was allegedly brutally assaulted by a passenger in Hopkins, Minnesota, on Saturday, in what his family says “appears to be a hate crime”. The driver, Mohamed Yusuf, is currently hospitalized and fighting for his life, his family told the Somali Brief , a digital news site run by two Somali American journalists . The driver’s cousin, Abdinasir Ali told the outlet that the alleged attack took place early Saturday after a passenger in Hopkins, a subur
noticias.texto:
A Somali-American Uber driver was allegedly brutally assaulted by a passenger in Hopkins, Minnesota, on Saturday, in what his family says “appears to be a hate crime”.
The driver, Mohamed Yusuf, is currently hospitalized and fighting for his life, his family told the Somali Brief, a digital news site run by two Somali American journalists. The driver’s cousin, Abdinasir Ali told the outlet that the alleged attack took place early Saturday after a passenger in Hopkins, a suburban city south-west of Minneapolis, asked Yusuf’s name and then said he did not like the name Mohamed.
The passenger allegedly then choked the driver from behind, took control of the car and used it to assault the driver. “He was run over multiple times with his own vehicle,” Yusuf’s son, Mustafa Osman, told the Somali Brief.
The badly injured driver was later found “a mile down the road in a ditch”, with broken legs and ribs, two collapsed lungs and a spinal injury, his son said.
The Hopkins police department said in a statement they are investigating the assault after officers responded to a report of a suspicious vehicle at 1.20am on Saturday.
“Officers located an adult male suspect nearby and took him into custody,” the police department stated. They noted preliminary information indicates the incident involved an Uber ride share interaction and that the investigation remains ongoing.
“This is a pure hate crime,” one member of Yusuf’s family at the hospital told the Somali Brief. “Our politicians created this hostile environment.”
The alleged assault comes after Donald Trump made racist rhetoric and lies about Somali Americans in Minnesota a central focus of his midterm campaign rallies, and the president’s inflammatory claims have been echoed by Minnesota Republicans.
House majority whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota, recently said on a conservative podcast: “I’ve got basically the Somali civil war that’s come to the state of Minnesota.”
The Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair-MN), community leaders, elected officials and ride-share driver groups were planning a press conference on Monday at the Hennepin County Medical Center to call for justice.
“Mohamed Yusuf should be home safe with his family, not fighting for his life after an attack fueled by hatred towards his Somali identity,” said Omar Fateh, a state senator in Minnesota, in a statement on social media. “We need answers and an immediate and transparent investigation.”
SEIU Local 26, a local labor union that organizes rideshare drivers, said in a social media post on the alleged attack: “We are shocked, angered and saddened by the news of the alleged attack that happened this weekend on Mohamed, a Minnesotan and Uber driver.”
A GoFundMe created on behalf of Yusuf and his family has already raised over $140,000. “As a result of this senseless assault, he suffered severe injuries and is now in a coma, fighting for his life,” the family wrote in the appeal for financial support.
“We are shocked and horrified by the details of this senseless attack,” a spokesperson for Uber said in an email.
“We banned the rider from the Uber platform, and we are keeping the driver and his loved ones in our thoughts. We stand ready to assist law enforcement with their investigation.”

noticias.titulo: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back as rebels advance
noticias.resumen: Forces aligned with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia are seeking to strengthen control over the interim capital Aden as the Iran-backed Houthis approach.
noticias.texto:
Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back as rebels advance
November 16, 2026
The Southern Armed Forces group allied with Yemen's UN-recognized government and backed by Saudi Arabia said Sunday they had repositioned themselves away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Why are troops moving away from Bab el-Mandeb?
The Southern Armed Forces said the repositioning is intended to secure the southern city of Aden, "and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the frontlines and addressing existing threats."
Aden, which has a population of over a million people, is the interim seat of the Yemeni government, formally known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC).
The Southern Armed Forces also intend to end the Houthi siege over the strategic southwestern city of Taiz.
Nearly two million people live in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
The siege is raising fears of famine for residents, as well as a possible medical crisis as hospitals face restricted supplies.
Houthis advancing towards Aden
The Houthis control much of northwest Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
The rebels are a Shiite militant group backed by Iran. The US, Canada and several other countries regard them as a terror organization.
The Houthis in September launched a rapid offensive against the PLC, seizing much of the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
It is also a key corridor for maritime trade and energy shipments.
The Houthis have taken control of the major port town of Mocha in September, firming their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The latest redeployment of the Southern Armed Forces is likely to give the rebels even more control over the strategic area.
Sources told AFP news agency that Houthi forces are now just 60 kilometers (less than 40 miles) from Aden.
The conflict between the Yemeni government and the Houthis has lasted for over 10 years.
The fighting in Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, has been fueled by the wider rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have been launching frequent attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, the rebels claimed that they targeted the King Khalid International Airport and financial district of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the alleged Houthi attack.

noticias.titulo: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
noticias.resumen: As tourism booms across Latin America, alternative forms of travel are gaining ground. Making your holiday more sustainable means rethinking who calls the shots, who invests and who benefits.
noticias.texto:
Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
November 15, 2026
Latin America is currently one of the world's most dynamic tourism regions. According to UN Tourism, the United Nations agency responsible for promoting responsible tourism, international arrivals in South America grew by 7% last year, while Central America saw a 5% increase, both above the global average.
But the boom comes at a price: overtourism. In some destinations, the sheer number of visitors is creating environmental and social problems, fueling tensions and raising questions about who really benefits from the business.
One famous example is Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in Peru, which lures up to 5,600 visitors a day. In 2025, Peru's official watchdog warned that more tickets were being sold than permitted, potentially putting the site at risk of being added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee has already expressed its concern.
In a bid to protect the Galapagos Islands and its bountiful ecosystems that inspired Charles Darwin, Ecuador doubled the entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024. Even so, pressure is mounting to construct new hotels and tourist apartments. And in Mexico City, the influx of tourists and digital nomads into neighborhoods such as Roma and Condesa has fueled protests over rising rents.
What can be done to make tourism more inclusive and sustainable? That's one of the industry's biggest questions. At ITB Americas, an international travel trade fair in Guadalajara, Mexico, DW spoke with three experts.
Sustainable travel moving from niche to mainstream
Richard Bazan is a regional manager for the Americas at Planeterra, a nonprofit organization that promotes and supports community-based tourism. He said several trends are emerging: group sizes are shrinking and travelers are seeking more intimate experiences.
"Where groups of 20 used to travel together, now it's four or five," he told DW.
So-called "nature-positive" tourism is also gaining traction, with travel programs that help fund, for example, reforestation projects. Bazan said even all-inclusive resorts are realizing that they can no longer shut themselves off from their surroundings. Instead, they need to offer authentic experiences that connect visitors with the destination.
"Community-based tourism is no longer a niche," he said.
Pressure for change is also coming from travelers themselves. According to Booking.com's 2025 annual survey, which polled 32,000 people in 34 countries, 93% said they wanted to make more sustainable travel choices. For the first time, more than half (53%) were aware of tourism's impact on local communities, not just the environment.
Communities know what's best for their land
Sarah Payne, director of the Reset Tourism Fund at the UnTours Foundation, pointed to the underlying problem. In the traditional tourism business model, most of the money generated never reaches local communities, the people who actually live with the influx of visitors.
"Access to financing is key, yet extremely difficult for communities," she explained. The financial products on the market tend to be expensive and inflexible, as tourism is considered a high-risk sector. Her foundation's fund offers low-interest loans with flexible repayment terms. Its guiding principle is that communities generally know what's best for their own land.
Sebastian Munoz, co-founder of Rutopia, a platform specializing in ecotourism and community-based tourism, has brought his experience from the nonprofit sector into social enterprise. His believes tours must be designed in partnership with communities so they feel a sense of ownership, rather than seeing them as something imposed from outside.
Bazan, meanwhile, thinks community-based tourism should not be approached as a humanitarian project, but through a market-driven lens: understanding what visitors are looking for and then planning hand-in-hand with the local community. In other words, building bridges between these two distinct worlds.
"It's not sustainable to create a product if no one comes to experience it," he said.
The challenge: Rethinking growth
The big question is how to grow without sacrificing sustainability. For Bazan, that decision doesn't belong to the tourism industry. Communities themselves must decide how they want to grow, and outside players should not pressure them. Their role, he said, is to amplify local voices, not to bring solutions or investments. "We have to learn to listen," he said.
The impact of community-based tourism is difficult to measure, Munoz acknowledged, because it has social impacts that go beyond the numbers. He cited the example of the Indigenous Mixtec community in Mexico that receives tourists interested in learning the local language. Suddenly, children who today speak only Spanish began joining the classes and asking their grandparents to teach them the language, too.
For Munoz, community-based tourism can be a powerful tool for valuing cultural and regional diversity. It's about creating value over the long term — and that, he said, is where the real experience for visitors lies.
The experts agree that change is slow. But they argue it's worth the effort: If there is more respect for local people and environments, in the end, everyone goes home happier.
This article was originally written in Spanish.

noticias.titulo: Zelenskyy urges removal of Starshield limits on Ukraine
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's government has said the throttling of satellite-based internet system prevents Kyiv from intercepting Russian attacks.
noticias.texto:
Zelenskyy urges removal of Starshield limits on Ukraine
November 15, 2026
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the US should remove any restrictions on the Starshield satellite internet system.
Kyiv is "counting" on the move due to severe damage to civilian infrastructure as a result of Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said, sharing photos from eight locations in his country.
"The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," Zelenskyy posted on his X account.
The satellite-based internet system was limited to slower speeds in October, with the limitations only being lifted due to criticism from Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said he had instructed several ministries, including the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to "work as closely as possible" with the US and Starshield owner Elon Musk's SpaceX. He added that the throttling of the system had helped Russian attacks.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine's interceptor drones are not effective due to losing connection with operators at the speed of 161 kilometers per hour. This results in the drones not being able to hit Russian drones or rockets.
Russian attacks continue
The past week, Russian attacks in Ukraine included more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles and cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said, calling Moscow's strikes "brutal" and saying they are "difficult to counter."
The US government and SpaceX gave in part contradictory answers to the question of who was responsible for the Starshield speed limit.
A Russian strike on the port city of Chornomorsk over the weekend resulted in six injuries and damaged energy infrastructure, local authorities said.
According to the authorities, a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks was hit, thus leaving some 41,000 customers without power on a temporary basis.
Six people were also injured after Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia, with one of those injured being a 2-year-old boy, according to Ukraine's emergency services.
Estonia said Russia was responsible for an attempted arson attack on a drone factory, with the border between the two countries to close, citing "clear evidence" Moscow is behind the attack.

noticias.titulo: Cape Verde's Jose Maria Neves wins presidential re-election
noticias.resumen: Cape Verde's President Jose Maria Neves has won re-election with 63.8% of the vote. Nearly 420,000 people were eligible to vote in the West African island nation.
noticias.texto:
Cape Verde election: Jose Maria Neves set to win second term
November 15, 2026
Cape Verde President Jose Maria Neves won re-election Sunday with 63.8% of the vote, according to provisional results from the country's electoral commission.
The 66-year-old Neves was seeking a second term as leader of the West African archipelago, which is known for its stable democracy.
His main challenger was 61-year-old Joana Rosa Amado, a former justice minister who secured around 31.6% of the vote.
Four other candidates also contested the election.
Some 420,000 people were eligible to vote in the west African archipelago, with the election being watched by about 150 observers from the Economic Community of West African States, the African Union and European Union.
Good governance
Cape Verde is made of ten volcanic islands located in the Atlantic Ocean about 600 kilometers (375 miles) off the coast of Senegal.
The island nation is known for its democratic stability and good governance, and its economy has been showing strong growth. The Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2026 index on global governance has the country in third place of Africa's 54 countries, with only Seychelles and Mauritius faring better.
Its political system is semi-presidential, with the prime minister being responsible for the executive. The president, in turn, is responsible for guaranteeing unity and upholding the constitution.
According to the World Bank, Cape Verde is an upper-middle-income country due to its growing tourism industry.
The challenges it faces range from social inequality, the islands' geographic isolation and the lack of traveling options between islands.
The increased cost of living, energy prices and youth unemployment also play a role.
The country became world renowned after its national team reached the 2026 World Cup's knockout stages despite taking part in it for the first time. Goalkeeper Vozinha, 40, became a world star due to his performance against later world champions Spain.

noticias.titulo: Pope Leo heads to the Amazon on the final leg of his South American tour
noticias.resumen: The religious leader warned that deforestation, illegal mining and pollution threaten the Amazon and its inhabitants. In Peru, the pope also demanded justice for Indigenous leaders killed defending their ancestral lands.
noticias.texto:
Pope Leo heads to Amazon on final leg of South America tour
November 15, 2026
Pope Leo XIV traveled from Peru's high Andes to the Amazon rainforest on Sunday.
During the final leg of his South American tour, the Roman pontiff warned that environmental destruction threatens both the region's fragile ecosystem and the communities that depend on it.
After visiting Cusco, the ancient Incan capital at an altitude of more than 3,400 meters (11,000 feet), the 71-year-old religious leader arrived in Pucallpa, a city on the Ucayali River in one of Peru's major deforestation hotspots.
"The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable," he said, calling on Catholics to resist the exploitation of the Amazon "with perseverance."
Meeting missionaries and representatives of Indigenous communities, the pope also condemned the killings of Indigenous leaders defending their ancestral lands.
"The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice," he said.
"The Church is with you," Leo told representatives of Indigenous communities and other peoples of the Amazon region.
Pope warns of threats to Amazon and its people
The pope warned that indiscriminate deforestation and water pollution were due to irresponsible exploitation of the Amazon's natural resources.
Peru lost 3.2 million hectares of forest between 2001 and 2024, according to government figures, an area roughly the size of Belgium.
The head of the Catholic Church, which has 1.4 billion followers worldwide, also voiced concern about the future of communities living in the Amazon.
"Protecting the Amazon rainforest cannot be separated from concern for the people who live there: Indeed, integral ecology, social justice and the spiritual life go hand in hand," he said.
Leo also pointed to large-scale drug trafficking as one of the issues undermining local communities' livelihoods.
"For us, the pope's arrival is a source of great joy, but it is also a great opportunity to make our demands, our grievances, and our problems heard," said Cecilio Soria, an Indigenous human rights activist.
Pope acknowledges suffering, contributions of Afro-Peruvians
Leo, originally from Chicago, served as the bishop of Peru's Chiclayo from 2015 until 2023, when he was called to the Vatican. He holds both US and Peruvian citizenship.
On Saturday, Leo held an open-air Mass in town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
He spoke with pleasure of returning to the "steep hills, ravines and fertile valleys, in a land with Andean roots, where the Inca Empire flourished and which is the cradle of a profound Christian faith."
Leo also visited the city of Zana, some 45 kilometers (28 miles) southeast, which is a major center of Afro-Peruvian society.
He said Zana "preserves the memory of generations of Africans who were torn from their homes and subjected to slavery."
"Many endured great suffering and humiliation. Dear brothers and sisters of African descent, today I want to express my affection and closeness to you," he said.
"Thank you for all that you contribute to the life of this church."
Leo apologized for the Church's role in transatlantic slavery in May.
Pope laments instability, violence in Peru
For both Pope Leo and the city's faithful, his stop in Chiclayo marked an emotional homecoming.
Speaking from his former cathedral, he addressed growing unrest and political instability a country where the homicide rate has doubled over the past five years and far-right President Keiko Fujimori was elected after promising to tackle crime.
"We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters," Leo said at the Cathedral of St. Mary in Chiclayo on Saturday.
"Yet, despite this darkness, which so often dims our hope and weakens our trust, God's gift continues to shine before our eyes."
Leo was scheduled to travel to the Peruvian capital, Lima, before heading back to Rome on Monday.

noticias.titulo: Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy
noticias.resumen: Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.
noticias.texto:
Polish activists face opposition as they make abortion more accessible
November 15, 2026
Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.
Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.
Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.
In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.
Pink lockers and PIN codes
Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.
Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.
The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.
Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.
"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.
Convicted of helping a woman to have an abortion
Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.
In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.
Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.
Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.
A 'complicated' legal situation
Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.
Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."
She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.
"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.
Opposition from Catholic groups
The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.
"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.
Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.
At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."
"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.
Support for women seeking an abortion
Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.
Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.
"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.
"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.
Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.
In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.
Rising support for right-wing parties
Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.
"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.
After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.
Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.
Two bills approved by parliament
In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.
One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.
The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.
Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.
According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.
Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

noticias.titulo: Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
noticias.resumen: NASA's Voyager 1, which is the furthest man-made object from Earth, is set to reach a new milestone this week. On Wednesday, the probe will be roughly 16 billion miles from Earth.
noticias.texto:
Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than anything else that humans have launched into space. On Wednesday, it's set to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that is one-light day away from Earth.
NASA is celebrating the occasion with the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day." Calling it a symbolic celebration, NASA is asking the public on Tuesday night to send Voyager's call sign V-G-R into the sky in morse code. Use a flashlight, phone light or anything that can blink a sequence.
If you want to take part:
V - Three quick flashes, one long flash
G - Two long flashes, one quick flash
R - One quick flash, one long flash, one quick flash
What exactly is a light-day?
A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, or more than 16 billion miles.
This NASA spacecraft has traveled for nearly 50 years, launching Sept. 5, 1977.
Over the course of its mission, Voyager 1 has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1979, it discovered a faint ring system on Jupiter. In 1980, the spacecraft took detailed photos of Saturn's rings and moons.
While on its journey, on Feb. 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook the U.S. space probe, Pioneer 10, becoming the most distant human-made object in existence. It and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only spacecraft to have operated outside of the heliosphere, which acts like a protective shield of the solar system.
Voyager 1 reached the interstellar boundary in 2012. Its interstellar mission continues to chart and measure the magnetic fields, particles and plasma waves outside the sun's heliosphere and the atmosphere of other stars.
Earlier this year, NASA elected to shut off Voyager 1's Low-energy Charged Particles experiment, or LECP, which has helped scientists map the structure of space, in order to save power. Scientists said this could keep the probe alive longer..
Voyager 1 has two science instruments still running: one that measures magnetic fields and another that listens for plasma waves.
In addition, the Voyager spacecraft is carrying the Golden Record – an interstellar "time capsule" to communicate Earth's story to extraterrestrials.
The gold-plated record contains 115 images, natural sounds such as surf, wind and animals, and spoken greetings in 35 different languages. Included are instructions, in symbols, on how to play the record and the origin of the probe.
Voyager 1 is estimated to reach "light-day status" at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, after 49 years, two months and 11 days of travel.

noticias.titulo: Who makes Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle jeans — and under what conditions?
noticias.resumen: Sydney Sweeney has great jeans, American Eagle Outfitters tells us. But who made them? And what are working conditions like in the garment factories of Pakistan and Bangladesh?
noticias.texto:
Who makes Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle jeans — and under what conditions?
KARACHI, Pakistan — In a slum dotted with shimmering pools of sewage, a garment worker nods in recognition as Sydney Sweeney slowly zips up her jeans in an American Eagle Outfitters advertisement playing on a smartphone.
But it's not Sweeney she recognizes — it's the jeans and jacket. This woman, a single mother, has worked on American Eagle production lines and seen those denim styles and similar models. "I know how all of them are made, because I have worked on them," she says.
When Sweeney's advertisement for American Eagle landed in July last year, with the tagline "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans," it triggered debate over whether it was a winking reference to eugenics because of Sweeney's va-va-voom beauty: thin, blonde, blue eyes, large breasts. Following the controversy, American Eagle said in a September 2025 statement that "'Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans' is and always was about the jeans." (Sweeney did not respond to NPR's request for comment.)
Missing from the debate over whether the advertisement was about jeans or genes was any significant reflection on who actually made the American Eagle jeans that Sweeney was wearing — as in, the workers. The majority of garment factories operate out of Asia, so most Americans will never meet the workers making their clothes or see the conditions they're made under.
The workers who make Sydney Sweeney's jeans
Workers like that single mother. She asks that we refer to her as S., the initial of her first name, because she fears her bosses at the garment factory where she works will fire her if she's identified. "If you raise your voice, they'll push you out," she says. "We are helpless."
S., a young woman, works at a factory run by a company called Artistic Garment Industries, where she says she's paid about $144 a month, a sum that supports her son and her mother.
She says the factory is "oppressively hot." It was 106 F outside when we met her, and she says the factory inside is even hotter. She says it's hard to leave her workstation to drink water because she has to meet her production targets. She says she has to check the quality of 1,000 to 1,600 pieces of clothing a day — and she's fainted three times this year. "I feel faint, and I can barely stand. I have no energy in my hands and feet," S. says. "They don't even let us sit down." But S. says she has no other options.
Artistic Garment Industries confirmed it makes clothes for American Eagle but tells NPR that it does not push out workers who complain about their working conditions. The company says it has a robust complaints system that workers can use and says it frequently checks on temperatures inside different parts of its factories.
In response to questions NPR sent to American Eagle, the company says it's "committed to working directly with our suppliers to protect the health, safety, and rights of workers. We take the concerns raised by workers — and those whom NPR interviewed — very seriously."
S. is one of around 20 workers we interviewed over the spring and summer in Bangladesh and Pakistan, two of the world's biggest global garment production hubs outside of China. Those men and women worked in five different factories. All of those workers asked NPR not to use their full names and to use only the initial of their first name, worried they'd lose their jobs or be blacklisted from future jobs if they were identified.
Inside the world of fast fashion
Although we focused on the American Eagle jeans worn by Sweeney for the 2025 campaign, the reporting led to a bigger issue: how fast fashion is made, because garment factories make clothes for multiple brands at once. Workers we met told us they made clothes for Levi's, Massimo Dutti, The Gap, H&M and American Eagle. They said it's common knowledge at the factories which brands they are making clothes for, in part because some workers are stitching on the labels.
The garment workers we spoke to offered strikingly similar accounts. And they echoed worker testimonies in multiple reports by labor and climate rights groups. The workers told us they're paid low wages, even as they're expected to reach what they say are unreasonably high production targets, often laboring in sweltering factories.
These are production targets like stitching 200 sleeves an hour or checking the quality of a thousand pieces of clothing a day. The workers we interviewed say they are unable to hydrate or cool down properly, even as extreme heat caused by climate change makes their workplaces and homes even hotter.
It can be four to six degrees hotter inside a factory, says Jason Judd, executive director of the Global Labor Institute at Cornell University, which researched heat inside garment factories and worker homes. "You've got all those bodies, all that material, all that machinery putting off heat. You've got ventilation problems."
"We're starting to see fainting, heat illness, exacerbation of chronic disease, even death," says Cara Schulte, a researcher at Climate Rights International. She authored two reports on the impacts of heat on garment workers.
Schulte says workers are put under that extreme pressure to reach production targets. A major reason is that brands demand their suppliers make enormous volumes of clothes on tight deadlines and on thin profit margins. And she says garment workers are vulnerable to the heat because they're clustered in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. She cites U.N. publications stating that those factories are "in areas that are warming faster than the global average, that are [already] incredibly hot and humid."
H&M, one of the brands that workers identified making, said it "put great effort" in ensuring fair payment to its suppliers and that labor costs are "excluded from the price negotiations of our product orders" to ensure that worker wages were not driven down.
Citing her own research, Schulte of Climate Rights International says garment workers are compelled to risk their health to survive. It's not a choice, she says. "Workers are not choosing to take these risks," she says. "They're being forced into them by poverty."
One worker's survival strategy
Like a woman who asks we call her R. When we met in February in the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, R. said she was working six days a week, at least 12 hours a day, for $140 a month at a garment factory run by a company called MBM, which makes denim clothes, including for Levi's. Her job is to stitch 150 pieces of fabric per hour, which are assembled into jeans.
R. says she's considered old for a garment worker — around 40 — and says she's slowing down. She says she's berated by managers who tell her, "Why aren't you speeding up your work?" She says, "If you're short by even a single piece, you face a lot of harassment."
R. says she's managed to meet her targets so far. "Allah has kept me safe," she says. She says friends of hers who could not meet their targets were fired by the company. To reach her targets, R. says, she stays at her station throughout her shift. "Even going to the washroom has become extremely difficult."
So despite Dhaka reaching 98 F this summer, R. says she doesn't drink much water to avoid the need to take bathroom breaks. There's no AC on the factory floor, but R. says managers run ceiling fans and keep windows open.
R. says that if workers feel faint, their bosses will let them rest in a sick room for about 20 minutes. But, she says, management will terminate employment if workers say say they feel sick too often, so she pushes herself to keep going.
MBM did not respond to questions from NPR about worker allegations.
Despite the issues she raised, R. says she works in a good factory. She says the pay is higher than other garment factories. And if she's terminated, she says the company will pay the wages, including overtime, that she's owed. But she doesn't want to be let go.
Taking the heat
These garment factories are blazing hot in part because it's expensive to retrofit them with air conditioners. A manager for MBM, who asked that NPR not use their full name because they are not authorized to speak to media, says that the company needs a brand to commit to purchasing long term in order for retrofitting the factory to pay off. The manager says no brand had committed to that kind of long-term business.
Conditions in Bangladesh are still better than in other garment hubs, because of the scrutiny after a building collapse killed more than 1,100 garment workers in 2013. Just three weeks after that disaster, a legally binding commitment called the International Accord emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh to protect worker health and safety. So far, 248 global brands and retailers have signed on, covering 2.8 million workers. A version of the International Accord was established in 2023 in Pakistan but has a smaller footprint.
There's meant to be more progress on protecting workers from extreme heat soon. Last December, the International Accord agreed to develop a protocol on heat stress. That means keeping workers cool will be an enforceable commitment for brands. For apparel companies in Bangladesh and Pakistan that have signed on to the accord, the International Accord staff will regularly inspect factories to ensure they're kept cool.
Judd, of the Global Labor Institute, says he believes there will be positive changes because the garment industry knows "they've got a problem — whether it's from a worker rights perspective, or from a business perspective, workers are slowing down, productivity is falling," he says. Either way, "you've got an interest in reducing the heat stress."
But for now, workers in Pakistan, in particular, described sweltering conditions, particularly in the port city of Karachi, one of the world's hottest garment hubs, according to the U.N.'s International Labor Organization.
In a dusty bazaar in Karachi, we met seven factory workers who mostly worked for two companies: Artistic Garment Industries — S.'s employer — and another called Artistic Milliners. Both produce clothes for big Western brands.
In their interviews with NPR, women who work, or worked, for Artistic Garment Industries described vomiting, fevers and fungal skin infections that they say were caused by the heat.
One young woman worker is I.
Her workday starts at 8:30 a.m. She says she is expected to work beyond her regular, nine-hour shift — often till 9 p.m. — and on Sundays as well, at some stretches. But she says she isn't paid all her overtime. I. also says supervisors on her floor berate workers if they leave their stations to drink water because it might cause them to miss their targets. So, I. says, "one person goes" to the water cooler and weathers the abuse, "fills a water bottle" and shares it with colleagues. I. says she gets about a glass full.
I. accuses the company of "eating" her money — and her health. "They exploit us," she says.
She says she suffers from dizziness and what she describes as a sense of fatigue and weakness. She pushes herself to work: "I can't lose my job — who else will support my family?"
Artistic Garment Industries contested these claims of unhealthful and exploitative working conditions. The company told NPR that it has a robust internal complaints system that workers could, and do, use. The company says it pays all overtime and does routine checks to ensure that the heat and humidity are not excessive on the factory floor. The company says it places water stations near workers to encourage them to hydrate and says it would not tolerate supervisors who pressure workers not to drink or use the bathroom.
Workers at Artistic Milliners described hot working conditions that badly impacted women and older male workers. One woman reported constantly feeling faint but said she pushed through. The workers said their supervisors let them drink water when they needed to, but they were pressured not to use the bathroom. Some workers said they were not paid for all the overtime they worked.
A 66-year-old former worker at Artistic Milliners, Sardar, said he was let go during the pandemic but had not been given compensation owed to him by the company. When NPR met him in June, he was homeless and relied on his children for meals. When we asked if he'd ever asked for charity, he began crying: "I'd feel ashamed if people thought I was begging."
Artistic Milliners did not respond to requests for comment about statements by Sardar and other workers. Parts of the company are certified through Fair Trade USA, a nonprofit organization that certifies companies that uphold high ethical standards for treatment of workers. NPR has sought comment from Fair Trade regarding allegations made by men and women who used to work for Artistic Milliners but has not received a response.
Answers from fast fashion brands
NPR also sent detailed questions to brands that workers said they made clothes for, alongside American Eagle.
Levi Strauss & Co. says it takes "allegations of worker rights violations seriously."
Inditex, the parent company of Zara and other labels, says Artistic Milliners, which makes clothes for one of its prominent brands, Massimo Dutti, was "subject to a corrective action plan." NPR contacted Inditex for clarification on what that corrective action plan entails but did not get a response.
Gap Inc. says it is "committed to supporting the rights and safety of workers."
H&M said in an emailed response that it has "required" AGI "to develop and implement corrective action plans to address the issues identified" by NPR: "Compliance with our requirements is a condition of our business relationship." H&M also said it recognized "the increasing risks associated with extreme heat" and is part of a pilot on heat stress in Pakistan conducted by the International Accord to develop "effective and sustainable solutions."
Those big brands partly ensure working conditions in factories are up to standard through regular audits. I. and other workers tell us they regularly saw auditors visiting their garment factory floors. They also tell NPR that supervisors give them advance warning. I. says that the supervisors "tell us to say that the working conditions are better than they actually are."
Anna Bryher is part of the workers' rights group Labor Behind the Labels, which published a report in July on the "clear mismatch" in the garment industry auditing system "between what the brands are saying and believing and hearing and what the workers report." Bryher says her findings suggest that the auditing system relied on by big brands is not working.
Artistic Garment Industries says workers may have confused regular updates informing workers of their rights with being told what to say at audits. The clothing brands that NPR reached out to did not comment on allegations regarding workers being told what to say during audits.
Some workers tell NPR that their supervisors warn them that if the workers were to criticize working conditions to auditors, the companies running the factories will lose business — and that they should paint a positive picture of their workplaces. "In other words," I. says, "they ask us to lie about everything."
With additional reporting by Hanan Biswas in Dhaka, Shahzaib Wahlah in Karachi and Abdul Sattar.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

noticias.titulo: Wedding industry representatives raise funds for children's hospital at annual gala
noticias.resumen: Representatives of the Hungarian wedding industry raised around 3 million forints for the Bethesda children's hospital at the 13th Hungarian Wedding Gala.
noticias.texto:
Representatives of the Hungarian wedding industry raised around 3 million forints for the Bethesda children's hospital at the 13th Hungarian Wedding Gala.
Representatives of Hungary's wedding industry raised around 3 million Hungarian Forints (€8.218,18) for a children's hospital at the 13th Hungarian Wedding Gala.
The events brought together over 400 photographers, videographers, wedding planners and other industry members from across at Budapest's Eiffel Art Studios.
The evening saw awards presented across 19 different categories, recognising achievements within the wedding industry.
Charity is an important tradition at the annual gala. This year, proceeds from ticket sales and raffle coupons went towards purchasing surgical drills for bone surgery for the Bethesda Children's Hospital.
Founder and chief organiser Katalin Landesz revealed that the cooperation with Bethesda "began with a tragic event".
“The son of our colleague suffered burns in a high-voltage electrical accident. The news deeply affected the entire industry, and that year we decided that the Wedding Gala would support her and her family to help her recover," Landesz told Euronews.
"This is now the third year we have supported the hospital. We either purchase another piece of life-saving equipment or take on a renovation project".
Earlier this year, more than 40 wedding industry professionals transformed the surgical departments at the Bethesda Children's Hospital in just two days.
The renovation brought a fresh look to the space, with decorations inspired by the four seasons and nearby city park. Every detail was thoughtfully designed to create a more child-friendly environment for young patients.
The volunteers also gifted furniture and custom designed curtains to the hospital and also renovated the washroom facilities.
